title: Unsupervised Learning Quick Revision: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction
summary: Night-before revision notes on k-means and choosing k, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, PCA with explained variance, t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation, and when unsupervised methods are the right tool.

chapters.title: Unsupervised Learning: The Mental Model
points: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data; two main jobs are clustering (group similar rows) and dimensionality reduction (compress columns)
No ground truth exists, so a clustering is judged by internal metrics and usefulness, not accuracy
Almost every method relies on a distance, so features on large scales dominate unless you standardise them first
Clustering groups rows; dimensionality reduction keeps most information in fewer features, and the two are often chained (PCA then k-means)
Core workflow: scale features, pick the method, tune its hyperparameter, validate with a metric plus a sanity check on cluster profiles

chapters.title: k-means and Choosing k
points: k-means loop: place k centroids, assign each point to the nearest centroid, move each centroid to its cluster mean, and repeat until assignments stop changing; it minimises inertia (within-cluster sum of squares)
Elbow method: plot inertia against k and pick the bend; inertia always falls as k grows, so the minimum is never the answer
Silhouette score ranges from -1 to 1; higher means tighter, better-separated clusters, and you pick the k with the highest average silhouette
sklearn: KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X_scaled); read labels_, cluster_centers_ and inertia_
Mistakes: forgetting to scale, assuming spherical equal-sized clusters, ignoring that results depend on random initialisation (use k-means++ and several n_init), and running it on categorical data

chapters.title: Hierarchical Clustering and DBSCAN
points: Agglomerative clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair, producing a tree called a dendrogram
Reading a dendrogram: cut horizontally at a height to get clusters; a long vertical gap before a merge suggests a natural number of clusters
Linkage sets what 'closest' means: single (chaining, elongated clusters), complete (compact clusters), average (compromise), ward (minimises variance increase, the usual default)

DBSCAN groups points by density using eps (neighbourhood radius) and min_samples; core points have at least min_samples neighbours within eps, border points sit near a core, and everything else is noise labelled -1

DBSCAN needs no k and finds arbitrary shapes plus outliers, but struggles with varying densities; hierarchical costs O(n²) memory so it does not scale to large data; choose eps from a k-distance plot elbow

chapters.title: PCA and Explained Variance
points: PCA projects data onto orthogonal axes (principal components) ordered by how much variance each captures; it is a linear method
Mechanism: centre the data, find the covariance eigenvectors (or use SVD); components are the eigenvectors and explained variance is the matching eigenvalue
explained_variance_ratio_ shows each component's share; keep enough components for a cumulative target such as 95%, or PCA(n_components=0.95) does it for you
Always standardise before PCA, otherwise large-scale features dominate the components; fit on training data only, then transform the test set
Components are linear mixes of features, which makes them hard to interpret; PCA also misses non-linear structure and is sensitive to outliers

chapters.title: t-SNE and UMAP for Visualisation
points: t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear methods that squash data to 2D or 3D to plot it, preserving local neighbourhoods
t-SNE key parameter is perplexity (roughly 5-50), the effective neighbour count; try several values because the picture changes
In a t-SNE plot, distances between clusters and cluster sizes carry no meaning, so never read them as real separation
UMAP is faster, scales better, keeps more global structure than t-SNE, and can transform new points; main knobs are n_neighbors and min_dist (umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1))
Use them for plots only, not as inputs to downstream models or as proof of clusters; set random_state for reproducibility and run PCA to about 50 dims first for speed

chapters.title: Unsupervised Methods Cheat Sheet
points: Pick by need: k-means for round clusters at scale, hierarchical for a dendrogram on small data, DBSCAN for odd shapes plus noise, PCA to compress, t-SNE/UMAP to visualise
Use unsupervised when labels are missing or costly: segmentation, anomaly detection, feature compression, exploration; use supervised when you have labels and a target
Metric picks: inertia and elbow for k-means, silhouette across any clustering, explained_variance_ratio_ cumulative for PCA
Always scale first; fit transformers on the training set only; fix random_state
Quick calls: KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10), AgglomerativeClustering(linkage='ward'), DBSCAN(eps, min_samples), PCA(n_components=0.95), TSNE(perplexity=30), umap.UMAP()
